kurz: Amylase is an [[enzym|enzyme]] that breaks starch down into sugar. It feeds the yeast, browns the crust and makes sweet potatoes sweet.
bild_im_kopf: Like a baker slicing long loaves: only in small pieces can everyone have some.
was_passiert: Starch is made of long chains of sugar units. Amylase cuts them into short pieces. Flour contains a little of it, malt contains a lot. In dough it gives the yeast food and leaves sugar over for a brown crust. Sweet potatoes contain their own amylase: cooked slowly, it works for longer and makes them sweeter.
warum_wichtig: Explains why bakers use baking malt, why slow-fermented doughs get a darker crust and why roasted sweet potatoes taste sweeter than boiled ones.
faustregeln: For a deep crust: a long, cool fermentation or a little baking malt.
Cook sweet potatoes slowly in the oven rather than boiling them fast.
Chewing starts the amylase in saliva: bread tastes sweetish after long chewing.

stellschrauben.wirkung: warmth keeps it working, boiling stops it

praxis.text: A cold overnight prove gives the amylase time: more sugar, a browner crust.
Sweet potatoes roasted for an hour at medium heat turn almost caramel-like.
